source_read: PDF scan, pp. 163-173 (all 11 pages read on the rendered page at 150 dpi; Tables 1-4 and Figures 1-2 on pp. 167-170 at 300 dpi; the OCR text layer was used only to locate passages, every number was read on the image)

claims.overstatement: No causal overstatement: the claim keeps 'associated' and says the design cannot show cause. Minor wording only. (1) 'Lifetime dependence was reported by 33.6%': dependence was a DSM-IV diagnosis derived from AUDADIS symptom questions, so 'met criteria for lifetime dependence' is more exact than 'reported'. (2) 'family drug problems, conduct problems and other psychiatric disorders were not measured': the paper states only that family history of drug use disorder was not measured (p. 166); conduct problems and psychiatric disorders are simply absent from the models and the paper does not say whether they were measured, so 'not adjusted for' is safer (from outside the paper, the NLAES did assess major depression). (3) 'the only prospective study the authors cite': true of studies of age at first use and later drug problems that the paper describes (Labouvie et al., 1997, p. 164); it also cites Kandel et al. (1986) and Bachman et al. (1985) on other consequences of adolescent use without describing their designs, so 'the only prospective study of age at first use the authors discuss' would be exact. (4) 'abuse without dependence fell from 28.9% to 13.6%' gives the endpoints correctly, but the fall is not steady (21.5% at 14, 25.1% at 16, 18.0% at 19).
claims.note: Every number from this source in the statement and magnitude was read on the rendered scan and matches: 1992, 42,862, about 92% and 97% (p. 165); ten classes and at least 12 uses (pp. 165-166); 6,447 and 15.6% weighted, 18.6% (SE 0.6) and 20.1% (0.6) (p. 167, Table 1); all nine dependence prevalences with their SEs (Table 3, p. 169); abuse 28.9% (1.9) and 13.6% (2.0) and the 11.1% (0.9) at 21 or older (Table 2, p. 168); coefficients -0.04 and -0.05 with SE 0.01 (Table 4, p. 170). Recomputed: exp(-0.04) = 0.961 and exp(-0.05) = 0.951, so the editors' conversion to odds ratios of about 0.96 and 0.95 per year is right; 18.6% + 20.1% = 38.7% (the paper's figure of about 40%). The abstract (p. 163) gives 4% for abuse and 5% for dependence, the reverse of Table 4, the Results (p. 170) and the Discussion (p. 171): confirmed. The 11.1% total for abuse at 21 or older cannot be a weighted total of the subgroups, being below both the male (13.9) and the female (11.7) value; it is the only such row in Tables 2 and 3; the text (p. 169) and Figure 1 repeat it; the claim rightly leaves it out. Not in the claim but relevant: in the subgroup models the age of first use was not significantly related to dependence among Black drug users (p. 171; 121 Black respondents with dependence); the Results give n = 1,273 for dependence as well as abuse (p. 168) while Table 3 gives 1,232; the Results list 'duration of drinking' as a covariate (p. 169) where Table 4 has duration of drug use; the n printed under Tables 2-3 are counts of people with the disorder, so the denominators for each age of first use are not reported; a Table 4 SE of 0.72 for male sex (dependence) is out of line with the others (0.07-0.09) and may be a misprint.

anchors.extracted: NLAES, 1992, fieldwork by the US Bureau of the Census; face-to-face interviews with 42,862 people aged 18 or older in the noninstitutionalized population of the contiguous US including DC; about 92% of selected households and 97% of randomly selected respondents in them took part (overall about 89%, editors' product); multistage design oversampling Black and 18-29-year-old adults.

anchors.locator: Method > Drug use, abuse and dependence assessment, 1st paragraph (begins p. 165)
anchors.extracted: AUDADIS; nonmedical use = use without prescription, in larger amounts, more often or longer than prescribed, or for another reason; ten classes (sedatives, tranquilizers, opioids other than heroin, amphetamines, cocaine/crack, cannabis, heroin, methadone, hallucinogens, other drugs such as inhalants); lifetime drug use = any drug in any class used at least 12 times.

anchors.locator: Method > Drug use, abuse and dependence assessment, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: DSM-IV lifetime abuse (1 or more of 4 criteria in any one year) and dependence (3 or more of 7 in any one year) derived per drug and combined into any drug abuse and any drug dependence; the two groups are mutually exclusive: lifetime abuse means abuse without lifetime dependence.

anchors.locator: Method > Drug use, abuse and dependence assessment, 4th and 5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Test-retest kappas (separate general-population study): any drug abuse or dependence 0.79 past year, 0.73 lifetime; age of onset 0.68 heroin, 0.69 sedatives, 0.77 cocaine, above 0.92 for tranquilizers, amphetamines, other opioids and cannabis. Family history of drug use disorder was not measured; family history of alcoholism was used as a control instead.

anchors.locator: Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
anchors.extracted: Prevalence by each year of age at first drug use (13 or younger to 21 or older); logistic regression adjusted for sex, race, age, duration of drug use, family history of alcoholism and current (past-year) vs former use; SUDAAN. About 16% (n = 6,447) were lifetime users; Table 1 weighted: use 15.6% (SE 0.2); among users abuse 20.1% (0.6), dependence 18.6% (0.6); dependence similar by sex (18.8, 18.4) and race (18.1, 18.7).

anchors.locator: Table 3, Total column (n = 1,232 with dependence); Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 on p. 170
anchors.extracted: Weighted lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence (SE) by age at first drug use: 13 or younger 33.6 (1.9); 14, 26.8 (2.4); 15, 25.4 (1.9); 16, 17.7 (1.3); 17, 15.1 (1.4); 18, 15.0 (1.5); 19, 13.4 (1.9); 20, 11.4 (1.8); 21 or older 13.6 (1.2). Figure 2 plots the same values (read off the figure). Among Black respondents 28.9 to 17.8, not uniform.

anchors.locator: Table 2, Total column (n = 1,273 with abuse); Figure 1; Results 2nd paragraph on p. 169
anchors.extracted: Weighted lifetime abuse (without dependence) by age at first use: 13 or younger 28.9 (1.9); 14, 21.5 (2.2); 15, 24.3 (1.9); 16, 25.1 (1.7); 17, 20.3 (1.7); 18, 17.7 (1.5); 19, 18.0 (2.4); 20, 13.6 (2.0); 21 or older 11.1 (0.9). The 11.1 lies below every subgroup value in its row (male 13.9, female 11.7, Black 12.6, nonblack 13.0), which a weighted total cannot do; the text (p. 169) and Figure 1 repeat 11.1.

anchors.locator: Table 4, row 'Age at onset of drug use'; Results, 4th paragraph (begins p. 169)
anchors.extracted: Age at first use entered as a continuous measure: abuse beta -0.05 (SE 0.01, p < .00003); dependence beta -0.04 (SE 0.01, p < .01); odds of dependence 4% and of abuse 5% lower per year of later onset; other terms: age 30-44, 45-64, 65+ vs 18-29, male, Black, family history of alcoholism, duration of drug use, former user. Editors' conversion: exp(-0.04) = 0.961, exp(-0.05) = 0.951.
The abstract gives reductions of 4% and 5% for lifetime drug abuse and dependence respectively, the reverse of Table 4 and of the Results and Discussion (abuse 5%, dependence 4%).

Subgroup models: abuse odds lower per year by 4% (males), 6% (females), 5% (nonblacks), 2% (Blacks); dependence lower by 5% (males), 2% (females), 4% (nonblacks); among Black respondents age of onset was not significantly related to dependence.

The one cited study that followed people (Labouvie et al., 1997): 15-year-olds followed for 13 years; onset of drug use did not predict drug-related adverse consequences at 30; the authors limit its weight because females were excluded, consequences covered only the 3 years before 30, and the measure was aggregate and not tied to clinical definitions. Next paragraph (pp. 164-165): Robins & Przybeck (1985) found earlier onset with greater risk, in 18-35-year-olds in St. Louis with DSM-III criteria.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st and 4th paragraphs; 5th paragraph (continues on p. 172); 6th paragraph on p. 172
anchors.extracted: Authors call age at first use a powerful predictor of lifetime abuse and dependence; ask whether the delay itself or, more likely, a combination of other factors lowers the risk, and whether early onset is a modifiable risk factor or a marker; call for prospective longitudinal studies from childhood beyond young adulthood (p. 172); restate early onset as a powerful predictor of long-term consequences (p. 172).

key_findings.note: Values match Table 3 and Figure 2. The editors' sums are right (62.5, 35.4, 25.0, 24.7), but the 21-or-older sum uses the impossible 11.1% abuse total; with any total lying between the male and female values (11.7-13.9) it would be about 25-28%.
Conversion recomputed: OR 0.951 (0.933-0.970) for abuse and 0.961 (0.942-0.980) for dependence per year.

reporting_issues.note: Checked on the 300 dpi render: it is the only row in Tables 2-3 where the total falls outside both subgroup pairs.
Recomputed: -4.10/1.31 gives z = 3.13, two-sided p = 0.0018 (0.0017-0.0019 allowing for rounding), not < .0005. The other printed p values in Table 4 are compatible with their betas and SEs.
Table 2 at onset 14: Black 30.3% vs nonblack 20.7%; the only age at which the Discussion's 'at each year' fails for race (men exceed women at every age).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high, driven by confounding (no measures of conduct problems, psychopathology, family drug problems; a covariate that may follow the outcome). The other domain judgments are reasonable.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the authors' language of a powerful predictor and of the development of disorders, used for a cross-sectional, recalled-onset association of about 4-5% lower odds per year; the abstract reverses the two figures; the 40% applies only to people who used at least 12 times.

missed: Replication timeline: the paper does not say where Robins & Murphy (1967) was done; St. Louis and the 18-35 age range belong to Robins & Przybeck (1985) in the paper's text (p. 165). Minor.

'The only prospective study the authors cite' (replication, where it stands) is exact only for studies of age at first use and later drug problems: the paper also cites Kandel et al. (1986) and Bachman et al. (1985) on other consequences of adolescent drug use, without describing their designs (p. 164). The same phrase is in the claim.

The card's can_establish says people who started younger 'more often reported' a disorder; the disorders were DSM-IV diagnoses derived from the interview, so 'more often met criteria for' is more exact (same point as in the claim).
